entries.title: Stop guessing auto scaling targets for TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI
entries.summary: Teams deploying custom text-to-speech models on Amazon SageMaker AI often guess at autoscaling thresholds, and a wrong guess either wastes GPU spend or breaches a latency SLO. This post deploys Kokoro-82M as a custom container and derives a measured autoscaling policy from two live-endpoint measurements, Q_max and T_total, instead of guesswork.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Stop guessing auto scaling targets for TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI

A traffic spike hits your self-hosted text-to-speech (TTS) endpoint, and requests start queueing. Latency climbs past your service level objective (SLO) right when the most callers are listening. The auto scaling policy behind that endpoint was supposed to prevent this, but the target value it scales on was a guess, and guesses like that fail silently until real traffic proves them wrong.

Get that number wrong, and it’s paid for in one of two ways, and neither shows up as an alarm. Guess too conservative, and the fleet runs GPU instances that sit mostly idle. That cost lands on every invoice but never trips an incident report. Guess too aggressive, and the fleet carries a risk nobody sees. Each instance holds more concurrent requests than it can serve inside its latency promise. Nothing looks wrong until a real traffic spike pushes queueing time past the SLO. That happens right when the most callers are listening. That’s the hidden gap. A policy that looks fine on the console can already be failing the people it’s supposed to serve.

In this post, we deploy Kokoro-82M, an 82-million-parameter TTS model, as a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) stacks handle the deployment. We replace guesswork with two measurements taken against the live endpoint. 

Q_max
is the highest concurrency one instance sustains before breaching the SLO, and 
T_total
is how long a scale-out takes end to end. We derive the scale-out threshold, scale-in threshold, and both cooldowns from those two numbers by arithmetic. Every number in this post comes from an actual deployment and measurement run of the aws-samples repository referenced in this post.

Why default auto scaling metrics don’t work for TTS

Most public guidance on Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling targets short synchronous request/response calls, or large language model (LLM) serving, where the natural metric is tokens generated per second. TTS synthesis fits neither pattern: a single request holds a connection open for several seconds with no token-generation loop to attach a metric to. Kokoro-82M is non-autoregressive, a StyleTTS2 derivative with an ISTFTNet decoder, trained adversarially rather than by autoregressive next-token prediction or iterative denoising. It produces a full utterance from one duration-aligned pass. There’s no generation loop to instrument with a per-token metric in the first place. What determines whether a TTS instance is overloaded is simpler than it sounds: how many requests are queued and executing on it right now.

The deployed policy scales on 

ConcurrentRequestsPerModel
, a native metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes itself rather than one this project’s own container code has to emit. Scaling on a metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes removes an entire class of failure where a custom metric configuration looks correct on paper but nothing is actually publishing to it.

ConcurrentRequestsPerModel
publishes a Maximum statistic over a 10-second window, a different quantity from the mean in-flight count a benchmarking client measures directly. The tooling accounts for this. At every rung of the concurrency ladder it measures both quantities against the same load and records the ratio between them. It then uses that ratio to convert the client-measured threshold into Amazon CloudWatch units before writing it into the deployable configuration. For the Kokoro-82M run in this post, the measured ratio came out to exactly 1.0 at every rung, so the client-measured and Amazon CloudWatch-reported thresholds match directly.

Solution overview

This solution deploys Kokoro-82M in a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, then replaces a guessed auto scaling target with one derived from two measurements taken against that live endpoint: 

Q_max
, the concurrency ceiling one instance serves inside the SLO, and 
T_total
, how long a real scale-out takes. A synthesis request flows through four layers: a client, the Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint, a custom container on a GPU instance behind that endpoint, and the Kokoro-82M model inside the container.

The container supports two wire transports: response streaming (

InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream
), which streams audio back as it’s synthesized so playback starts before the utterance finishes, and bidirectional streaming (
InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream
), which holds one long-lived session open for multiple messages.

Running Kokoro-82M in a custom container, rather than behind a managed inference toolkit, is what makes the rest of this post possible. A container you control can enforce its own admission limits and expose the exact concurrency signal Amazon SageMaker AI already publishes, instead of retrofitting a borrowed metric onto a workload it wasn’t built for. The AWS CDK stacks that deploy this endpoint only attach auto scaling resources once a real, measured 

plan
exists for the model, so a guessed configuration can never reach production silently. The rest of this post is that measurement.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, you need:

  • An AWS account with permissions to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories, and Amazon SageMaker AI resources.
    • Note: the sample container pins an earlier PyTorch with a known advisory (
      PYSEC-2026-2286
      , fixed in torch 2.10.0). Review and upgrade the pin before any non-proof-of-value use.
  • AWS CDK v2, installed and bootstrapped in your target account and region.
  • Python 3.11 or later, uv, and Docker to build the container image.
  • A 
    ml.g5.xlarge
    service quota with at least one spare slot above your baseline before running the scale-out measurement in this post.
  • The deployment code from the GitHub repository referenced in this post.

Walkthrough

By the end of this walkthrough, you will have a live Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling policy for Kokoro-82M, derived entirely from two measurements taken against your own endpoint rather than from a guess.

Deploy the endpoint stacks

The endpoint deploys through three AWS CDK stacks, applied in order: 

SpeechFoundationStack
creates the IAM roles and the Amazon S3 bucket that caches model weights, 
SpeechModelCacheStack
syncs a model’s Hugging Face weights into that bucket once, and 
SpeechEndpointStack
builds the container image, pushes it to Amazon ECR, and creates the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint.

The gate on the third stack keeps a default, unmeasured scaling configuration from reaching production. 

scaling_enabled
is a static flag, true whenever 
max_instances
is configured greater than 
min_instances
, and it says nothing on its own about whether the numbers behind it were ever measured. The stack adds a second, independent check at synthesis time: does a real, feasible 
plan
artifact exist for this model? Only when both conditions hold does the stack synthesize scaling resources: an 
EndpointAutoscaling
construct that wires the scaling policy and alarms, and an 
EndpointObservability
construct that adds the dashboards and alarms used to monitor it. A model with 
scaling_enabled=True
but no measurement behind it gets the same no scaling resources output as one with 
scaling_enabled=False
.

The project’s CLI wraps the three stacks behind a single command, applying them in dependency order:

SpeechModelCacheStack
runs an AWS CodeBuild project that syncs the model’s Hugging Face weights into the cached Amazon S3 bucket once. A cold endpoint start doesn’t need to pull them from the internet. Gated by the preceding 
scaling_enabled
check, 
SpeechEndpointStack
builds the container image, pushes it to Amazon ECR, and creates the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint.

The methodology packages as a command-line tool chain, run in a fixed order:

Step 1: Check for drift

drift
runs first, every time, before anything that costs money or holds an endpoint under load. It’s a read-only reconciliation between what’s actually deployed (scalable targets, scaling policies, alarm states) and what the config file says should be deployed. An orphaned policy from an earlier model, or a stopped or canceled 
qmax
or 
ttotal
run, would otherwise silently move capacity mid-measurement and corrupt the numbers being measured.

A clean result reports no mismatches and exits with a preflight-ok status, clearing the way for 

qmax
. A stopped or canceled 
qmax
or 
ttotal
run is the most common source of a reported mismatch, because it can leave auto scaling frozen on a single instance. 
uv run tts-bench thaw --endpoint speech-kokoro-82m
restores the deployed policy before you proceed, since 
qmax
and 
ttotal
both assume the deployed state matches the config file exactly.

Step 2: Measure Q_max, the concurrency ceiling

Q_max
is the largest concurrency, requests queued plus requests executing on one instance, at which a request still reaches first audio byte inside the SLO at the 95th percentile. It’s measured with a closed-loop load ladder: hold a fixed concurrency 
N
exactly, and walk 
N
upward one rung at a time until the SLO breaks. A closed loop avoids coordinated omission, the flaw in fixed-arrival-rate tests where a slowing server makes the client send fewer requests instead of surfacing real queueing delay.

--dry-run
prints the schedule and a wall-clock estimate with zero AWS calls, so you can budget the roughly 36-minute cost of a live run first. The live command freezes auto scaling and pins capacity to one instance for the duration, restored automatically on exit, so the number it produces is a genuine per-instance ceiling.

The load ladder recorded the following results:

Q_max

Q_max = 50
, and it’s a bracketed result: rung 60 actually crossed the SLO, which makes 50 a real ceiling rather than a lower bound. The same run measured the uncontended service time, the time one request takes with no queueing at all: mean 61.3 ms, p95 66.1 ms. That number drives a second, independent alarm described later in this post.

Step 3: Measure T_total, the real scale-out time

T_total
is how long it takes, wall clock, from the moment more capacity is requested to the moment that capacity serves healthy traffic. It’s measured by forcing a scale-out directly, bypassing the deployed policy’s own detection logic, then timestamping every distinguishable stage.

ttotal
requires the 
qmax
artifact as input, since its recovery judgment reads off that ladder’s own measured rungs, and refuses to run against a ladder measured on a different wire transport.

The forced scale-out broke down into eight measured stages:

StageDurationShare of 
T_total
capacity requested to desired_set30.0 s9.4%
desired_set to instance visible in logs180.8 s56.5% (dominant)
instance visible to container started3.7 s1.2%
container started to framework_init0.0 s0.0%
framework_init to weights_ready6.5 s2.0%
weights_ready to warmup_done1.0 s0.3%
warmup_done to in_service20.7 s6.5%
in_service to traffic recovered47.4 s14.8%
measured total (t_total_s)260.2 s

T_total, planned against320.2 s

The dominant stage is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance provisioning plus the container image pull, at 181 seconds, 56 percent of the planned-against total. The highest-impact way to reduce 

T_total
isn’t application code, it’s reducing image size or using warm capacity pools. Everything downstream of “instance visible in logs” is a comparatively small 79 seconds combined.

The 60-second addition on top of the measured 260.2 seconds isn’t measured in this run. It’s bounded from the policy’s own configuration (alarm evaluation period times evaluation periods, plus cooldown), because this run bypassed the policy’s detection logic on purpose to isolate pure provisioning time. 

plan
sizes surge headroom against the full 320.2-second total, because that reaction time is a real part of any production scale-out even though this measurement excluded it.

Step 4: Derive the deployed policy with plan

plan
is the only command that never touches AWS. It reads the 
qmax
and 
ttotal
artifacts, combines them with two operator-chosen inputs, an SLO of 3,000 ms p95 TTFAB and a surge ratio of 1.25x (the fleet tolerates traffic growing 25 percent within one scale-out cycle without breaching the SLO), and does the following arithmetic. It then prints a report with a verdict for each finding: 
ok
, 
warn
, or, for a genuinely infeasible plan, 
stop
.

The 

--peak-rps
flag (5,000 requests per second here, alongside an assumed trough of 10) sizes the fleet’s instance count. It doesn’t factor into the threshold arithmetic below.

C_scale_max
is the concurrency at which one more instance is added, below 
Q_max
by the surge fraction 
h
, so the fleet still has queue headroom when it asks for more capacity. 
C_scale_min
is the concurrency at or below which one instance is removed, set at 
(1 - 2h)
of 
Q_max
so scale-in triggers only once load has fallen well below where scale-out would trigger again.

The final deployed configuration, exactly as produced by the tooling:

The two cooldowns are asymmetric on purpose. Scaling out is cheap to be wrong about: worst case, you paid for one instance you didn’t need for thirty extra seconds. Scaling in isn’t symmetric in cost, since capacity removed and later needed again costs a full 

T_total
(320 seconds) to replace. The scale-in cooldown is set to roughly three times 
T_total
, so a scale-in decision only fires once load has genuinely, sustainedly dropped.

The container’s own admission control separately enforces 

queue_max_depth=50
, equal to 
Q_max
: past that depth, a request is refused immediately with a 
503 queue_saturated
response rather than left to queue past the point it could meet the SLO. A 
FirstChunkLatencyP95
alarm, thresholded at 65 ms (the measured p95 service time at concurrency 1), watches service time on an instance already serving, tighter than the end-to-end SLO, which includes queuing.

Two findings from the Kokoro-82M run are worth including, because they’re the tool correctly surfacing a known, accepted trade-off rather than a defect:

  • surge_survival
    (warn): Holding 
    C_scale_max
    (37.5) against 
    Q_max
    (50) puts one instance at 97.4% utilization the moment a scale-out triggers, and a replacement takes a full 
    T_total
    to arrive. The surge ratio reserves extra queue slots, but surviving a real surge is about flow, how fast the queue drains, and there’s little flow headroom left at 97.4 percent utilization.
  • scale_in_safety
    (warn): Removing one instance from a fleet of 
    N
    multiplies every remaining instance’s concurrency by 
    N / (N-1)
    . Scale-in stays stable only once that ratio holds under 
    C_scale_max / C_scale_min
    (1.5 here), which requires 
    N >= 3
    . With a floor of 1 instance, a scale-in from 2 to 1 lands the survivor at exactly 
    Q_max
    , right back at the ceiling that triggers another scale-out. The long cooldown damps this flapping without eliminating it. Raising the floor to 3 would remove it structurally, at the cost of standing capacity during low traffic.

Every 

qmax
or 
ttotal
artifact’s file name encodes the configuration it was measured against, instance type and container image digest condensed into a slug (for example, 
g5xlarge-8b1b96bc
). 
ttotal
and 
plan
both refuse to pair artifacts whose fingerprints disagree. That’s downgradable to a warning with 
--allow-config-mismatch
, but refusal is the default.

Step 5: Confirm the deployed policy with validate

validate
is the last command in the chain, and the second one, alongside 
drift
, that never mutates anything. It compares the scaling policy actually deployed against the values in the 
plan
artifact, confirming the two match before you treat the configuration as live.

A clean result confirms 

scaling_target_value
, 
scale_in_threshold
, and both cooldowns on the deployed scalable target match what 
plan
derived. Any mismatch means the deployed policy and the measured plan have drifted apart, and should be resolved before relying on the endpoint’s auto scaling behavior.

Testing and validation

Every 

qmax
, 
ttotal
, and 
plan
artifact referenced in this post is a committed file in the repository, not a one-off local output. The preceding worked example, including every number, is independently reproducible by re-running 
plan
against the two committed measurement files, with zero AWS calls and zero new spend:

Clean up

To remove the resources created in this walkthrough, tear down the stacks in reverse order with a single command:

speech-infra destroy
removes the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, endpoint, and any auto scaling or Amazon CloudWatch resources attached to it. It doesn’t empty the Amazon S3 bucket that caches model weights or delete the Amazon ECR repository holding the container image, since both can be shared across models. If you no longer need them, empty and delete the Amazon S3 bucket and remove the Amazon ECR repository manually, since a stored model checkpoint and container image continue to incur small storage charges until removed.

Conclusion

Deploy Kokoro-82M as a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, and replace guesswork with two measurements taken against the live endpoint: 

Q_max
, the highest concurrency one instance sustains before breaching the SLO, and 
T_total
, how long a real scale-out takes. You derive the scale-out threshold, scale-in threshold, and both cooldowns from those two numbers by arithmetic. Scaling on 
ConcurrentRequestsPerModel
, a native, AWS-published metric, and measuring its unit conversion directly rather than assuming it, is what keeps this configuration tied to real concurrency.

The result is an auto scaling policy where every number traces back to a real measurement against your own endpoint, not an assumption carried over from a different workload shape. That distinction is what turns a config-file guess, one that silently overpays or silently breaches its SLO, into a policy you can defend with a specific concurrency ceiling and a specific scale-out time, both measured, not asserted.

Nothing about this four-number model, SLO and surge ratio chosen, 

Q_max
and 
T_total
measured, the rest derived, is specific to TTS. It generalizes to latency-sensitive, concurrency-bound, real-time Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints. For example, a real-time image-embedding endpoint that holds each request open through a GPU forward pass is bound by the same concurrency ceiling, not by a throughput metric. The same 
qmax
/
ttotal
/
plan
chain applies unchanged. The real bottleneck there is concurrent in-flight requests rather than a throughput metric borrowed from a different workload shape. The specific numbers here, 
Q_max=50
and 
T_total=320s
, are true for Kokoro-82M on 
ml.g5.xlarge
. They will differ for a different model or instance type. The methodology and tooling that produce them don’t. The five-command tool chain, 
drift
, 
qmax
, 
ttotal
, 
plan
, and 
validate
, carries over unchanged to the next model you deploy this way.

Clone the sample repository, then run the five-command chain, 

drift
, 
qmax
, 
ttotal
, 
plan
, and 
validate
, against your own endpoint to produce a measured policy. Review the Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling documentation to adapt the thresholds to your SLO, and open the SageMaker AI console to watch the policy react to live traffic. If you’d like help building a similar measurement-driven deployment, contact your AWS account team.

entries.title: How Rescale built an AI triage agent with Strands Agents and AI-DLC
entries.summary: Rescale used the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) framework on AWS, with Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock, to build an intelligent test-triage agent in weeks. Learn how AI-DLC structures AI-assisted development and how Rescale is scaling the practice across its engineering organization.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How Rescale built an AI triage agent with Strands Agents and AI-DLC

Every engineering team knows the ritual, and Rescale was no exception. A nightly test suite fails. An on-call engineer pulls the logs, classifies the root cause, and routes it to the right team, only to repeat the process the next morning. At scale, across distributed services and dozens of repositories, this ritual becomes a full-time job hiding inside an on-call rotation.

Rescale is the digital engineering platform built for the AI era. R&D and engineering teams across aerospace, automotive, energy, life sciences, semiconductor, and manufacturing use the Rescale platform to accelerate innovation, bringing intelligent HPC, advanced modeling and simulation, agentic digital engineering, and AI physics together on a single platform.

Beyond coding, Rescale uses AI across the engineering lifecycle, from planning and design through implementation, testing, review, and operations, while keeping engineers accountable for the result. AI can propose and execute, but people define scope, validate the work, and approve production changes. Engineers can then focus on architecture, product judgment, and the context required to operate complex distributed systems.

In this post, we show how Rescale used the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) framework on AWS to build an intelligent triage agent. They went from problem definition to staging deployment in five days, and to production within weeks. The post also covers how Rescale is extending AI-DLC across their engineering organization.

The challenge

As Rescale’s platform grew, so did the operational overhead of keeping it running. Engineers were spending significant time on a repetitive but critical task: classifying automated end-to-end test failures. Hundreds of test cases run in the suite, and when failures appeared, every alert, bug report, and escalation needed to be classified, prioritized, and routed to the right team. After routing, engineers would need to gather evidence from multiple logging and monitoring systems, along with several source repositories before debugging could even begin. Passing end-to-end tests were required to deploy services to production and thus debugging these system failures was in the critical path to getting new changes to production.

In the manual workflow, engineers moved from the test report to logs, historical patterns, and source code to classify failures and identify the likely owning team. Because these integration tests gate weekly production releases, unresolved failures could pull several teams into hours of coordination before a deployment was allowed to proceed.

The team had a clear idea of what a solution looked like: an intelligent agent that could classify and route issues automatically. What they were looking for was a structured way to go from that understanding to a working system in production, with enough structure to extend the approach to other use cases afterward.

Why Rescale chose AI-DLC

Rescale’s triage agent was a well-scoped problem with a tight timeline. The team needed a development approach that could move at that pace without skipping the architectural decisions that would determine whether the system worked in production.

The AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) is an open source, AI-centric methodology for software development built around two ideas:

  • AI executes, humans decide: AI generates work plans, writes code, and proposes architecture, but it surfaces decision points and asks clarifying questions rather than guessing. Humans validate and steer at each step.
  • Team sessions replace async handoffs: Instead of one person building alone and requesting review later, AI-DLC uses focused group sessions: Mob Elaboration (defining requirements together) and Mob Construction (building together while AI handles implementation). Decisions happen in real time.

AI-DLC fit because the hard part wasn’t writing code. It was making sure the AI understood what the team wanted to build. In mob sessions, Rescale engineers answered the AI’s questions together and approved each plan before the AI moved on, so nothing was left to assumptions.

Solution overview

Rescale’s triage agent automates the classification and routing of nightly end-to-end test failures. It runs as a step within Rescale’s existing Argo Workflows continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). When a nightly Playwright suite of hundreds of test cases produces failures, the pipeline triggers the triage agent pod.

The agent performs the following steps:

  • Invokes Claude Opus 4.8 on Amazon Bedrock to classify each failure into a root cause category: infrastructure issue, code bug, flaky test, or environment problem.
  • Retrieves relevant historical failure patterns from a knowledge base for additional context.
  • Queries pod logs through Model Context Protocol (MCP) for runtime evidence supporting the classification.
  • Generates a structured remediation report with specific file references, function names, and recommended fixes for engineer review before any action is taken.

The agent completes this workflow in seconds and outputs directly into the team’s existing reporting pipeline. The following diagram shows how these components fit together:

The AI-DLC workshop experience

The engagement was structured as a five-day, in-person workshop. AWS architects guided the build while Rescale engineers worked hands-on-keyboard, co-building in real time.

Inception phase (days 1–2): From vision to validated requirements

The team started by scoping requirements, capturing the intent in a vision document and a technical environment document that grounded the work before any building began. That intent began as a single statement, “We want AI-powered test triage that classifies failures and recommends remediation”. Working collaboratively in mob format, the team answered 20+ clarification questions generated by AI. This produced a scoped requirements document with Phase 1 boundaries explicitly defined and Phase 2 items deferred. Five user stories were consolidated into four units of work:

  • Knowledge base for historical failure patterns.
  • AI triage agent as the core classification and remediation engine.
  • Argo Workflow Integration for trigger, infrastructure, and deployment.
  • Evaluation Harness for accuracy measurement and regression gating.

Human decisions drove the critical boundaries: what belongs in Phase 1 versus Phase 2, priority ordering, and deferred features like automated pull request (PR) generation.

Construction phase (days 2–4): Architecture to running code

The team defined interface contracts and data schemas, completed functional and non-functional design questions, and signed off on the architecture. Two architecture pivots emerged during the build, and the team validated each one before changing course.

First, the team planned to host the agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, then moved it to Amazon EKS, where Rescale already runs its Argo Workflows CI/CD pipeline. Keeping the agent in the existing cluster meant no new runtime to operate and a direct trigger path from Argo. Second, in the early build the agent pulled log evidence from a third-party logging service through MCP. The team moved log retrieval to Amazon CloudWatch, which simplified the dependency chain. The MCP pattern stayed the same. Only the source behind it changed. Because AI-DLC keeps requirements and design decisions in shared documents, the team updated them in place and kept building without losing context.

The agent was built using the Strands SDK, supporting concurrent failure analysis with structured output in JSON and HTML, containerized on Amazon EKS.

By Day 4, the full pipeline was running in staging: Argo workflow trigger, triage agent pod, MCP log query, knowledge base retrieval, and structured triage output.

Operations phase (day 5): Evaluation and handoff

The team built a PyTest-based evaluation framework with live and stubbed test modes, establishing an initial classification-agreement baseline to measure the agent against and improve from. The agent was demoed live to Rescale’s CTO and VP of Engineering, correctly classifying both an infrastructure failure and a real code bug with specific file-level fix recommendations.

How AI-DLC scaled rigor to complexity

Not every unit of work gets the same treatment. The knowledge base needed minimal design and deployed using Terraform in hours. The Triage Agent got full rigor: architecture review, interface contracts, 12 design questions, and iterative code review. Argo Integration focused on infrastructure contracts and IAM. The Evaluation Harness used lightweight design but heavy implementation. AI-DLC matched depth to complexity automatically.

By the end of Day 5, the agent was live in staging, processing real test failures with a measured accuracy baseline and a clear path to production.

Production outcomes

The triage agent has been running in production since the workshop. It automatically classifies nightly end-to-end test failures, replacing manual first-pass triage with an automated first pass that engineers validate. For each failure, the agent generates a structured remediation report with actionable next steps rather than raw logs. The agent’s classification agreement with human triage has risen from 44% at initial deployment to 68% today. It continues to improve as the team iterates on the golden dataset and prompt engineering.

Since the triage agent entered production, the team has measured a 20% decrease in time blocking production deployment while test failures are analyzed. Because these tests gate Rescale’s weekly production releases, that reduction shows up directly in how quickly changes reach production. Engineers also spend less of the on-call rotation on repetitive classification.

Life after the workshop: From one agent to an AI-first practice

The workshop delivered one production agent, but its larger effect was on how Rescale approaches engineering work. The triage agent is part of a broader push at Rescale to deliver digital engineering capabilities for the AI era. Internally, Rescale is applying these same benefits realized from AI across its own engineering organization. AI-DLC gave Rescale’s engineers a structured, repeatable way to put that direction into practice.

Scaling AI-DLC across the organization

Rescale is evaluating an internal AI-DLC Center of Excellence, a small group that codifies best practices and helps other teams adopt the methodology independently.

The engineers who participated are already applying what they learned. One of the engineers noted that the process “will be part of my workflow going forward,” not only for building agents, but for any complex development work where AI can contribute.

Broader AI-native development

Rescale is now incorporating AI-DLC into the standard software development lifecycle for new engineering simulation products. The framework brings simulation-domain expertise, product requirements, platform architecture, validation, and operations into one structured design process. Teams resolve key questions early, capture reviewed decisions in executable specifications, and give coding agents focused work with clear acceptance criteria. This shortens the path from product concept to validated implementation while engineers remain accountable for product correctness.

The same approach is already being used in product-enabling platform work and agent systems:

  • HPC simulation application catalog management.
  • Container vulnerability tracking and remediation for government compliance requirements.
  • Workflow-based cloud coding agents.

Conclusion

For the triage agent, the most useful output of AI-DLC was not the code itself. It was the structured path from an initial idea to a reviewed system design: clarifying questions, scoped requirements, and evaluation criteria.

That specification gave coding agents a narrower, better-defined problem to solve. Instead of asking an agent to infer the architecture while implementing it, the team could use agents for focused construction against decisions that humans had already reviewed. The result was more focused, reviewable output that was easier to integrate and improve. For Rescale, that is the repeatable pattern: use AI-DLC to structure the design conversation, turn the decisions into a specification, and then use coding agents to accelerate implementation.

Key takeaways

  • Start with a real problem. Rescale’s triage agent succeeded because it solved an engineering challenge. The problem drove the solution, not the other way around.
  • Human oversight accelerates, not decelerates. Every architecture pivot that improved the system came from human validation of AI proposals. The mob format, where AI generates and humans validate, is faster than working alone.
  • The AWS stack provided each layer the agent needed. Amazon Bedrock supplied foundation-model access for classification in an environment Rescale was already using, so the team could build the triage workflow without taking on additional model-infrastructure overhead. The Strands SDK provided the agent framework, and Amazon EKS hosted the containerized agent within Rescale’s existing pipeline.

entries.title: Securing Quick access from corporate networks with AWS PrivateLink
entries.summary: Learn how to connect on-premises data sources to Amazon Quick privately with AWS PrivateLink, keeping analytics traffic off the public internet. This walkthrough covers VPC endpoints for user and API access, VPC connections for data sources, DNS and endpoint policies, identity federation, and enforcing VPC-endpoint-only access for compliance.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Securing Quick access from corporate networks with AWS PrivateLink

When enterprise data sits behind a corporate firewall or in a private on-premises data center, there’s no direct network path from AWS, even though the AI agents and dashboards in Amazon Quick can query virtually any data source. Administrators must make sure their sensitive enterprise data isn’t exposed to the public internet while being accessible for AI-driven insights and actions.

For many enterprises, routing traffic over the public internet introduces unacceptable risk. Regulatory frameworks such as HIPAA, FedRAMP, and PCI-DSS often mandate that sensitive data remain within controlled network boundaries. Even where compliance isn’t the primary driver, exposing internal data paths increases the attack surface, complicates audit trails and introduces variable latency that can degrade the user experience.

This walkthrough shows you how to connect on-premises data sources to Amazon Quick privately, without traffic traversing the public internet. It assumes you already have AWS Direct Connect or an AWS Site-to-Site VPN linking your on-premises environment to your virtual private cloud (VPC). From that foundation, we configure VPC endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink so that Quick can reach your private resources over the AWS backbone, then layer security groups and VPC endpoint policies for defense in depth.

By the end, you will have a network architecture that keeps traffic between Quick and your on-premises data sources off the public internet, reducing the attack surface, providing consistent low-latency connectivity, and giving you a clear audit trail for compliance.

Amazon Quick and establishing private network connectivity

Amazon Quick is an AI-powered workspace that brings search, analytics, research, and automation into a single conversational experience. Understanding which components reach your private network, and how, determines the architecture in the sections that follow.

Data access in Amazon Quick falls into two paths. User-facing traffic covers anyone opening the Quick console, interacting with a dashboard, making an API call, or using Quick Desktop. All this routes through VPC endpoints (see VPC endpoints for user and API access), keeping user sessions off the public internet.

Data-fetching traffic is when Quick itself reaches into your network to pull data. This is handled by VPC connections (see VPC connections for data source access), and it’s where most of the architectural decisions lie. The features and integrations that initiate data-fetching connections are:

  • Amazon Quick Sight queries on-premises databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, and others) directly through ENIs placed in your VPC. This is the heaviest consumer of VPC connections.
  • Amazon Quick Flows and Amazon Quick Automate are separate automation features. Flows handle repeatable tasks. Automate handles complex, multi-system orchestration with human-in-the-loop. Both invoke action connectors, including MCP servers hosted privately in your VPC. Any workflow that calls an internal API routes through this path.
  • Quick Agents underpin all conversational interactions and can invoke action connectors directly. When a custom agent calls a privately hosted MCP server or internal API, traffic flows through the VPC connection.
  • Amazon Quick Index builds a unified search layer across connected sources such as Confluence, SharePoint, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). For data inside your VPC or on premises, knowledge base VPC connections are currently supported only for Amazon Redshift. Sources such as Confluence, SharePoint, Box, Google Drive, OneDrive, and Amazon S3 can’t use a Quick VPC connection today (see Supported VPC data sources). You can still restrict Amazon S3 bucket access to a VPC endpoint through a bucket policy, which is a separate mechanism.
  • Amazon Quick Research accesses enterprise sources behind the firewall alongside public internet data for its citation-backed reports, using the VPC connection when reaching private sources.
  • Apps in Quick build interactive web applications on top of structured data and action connectors, inheriting the same VPC connectivity as Quick Sight and Flows.
  • Quick Spaces organize content from the preceding features but don’t initiate their own data connections.

These two traffic paths require two distinct private connectivity mechanisms that work together:

  • VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink): Handle user-facing traffic such as accessing the Quick website, making API calls, and administrative access. These keep user traffic off the public internet.
  • VPC connections: Handle data source traffic. Amazon Quick reaches into your VPC (and by extension, your on-premises network) to fetch data from databases, Amazon Redshift knowledge base sources, and internal APIs. These are configured within the Quick console.

Configuring private connectivity

This section walks through the four building blocks in order: VPC endpoints for user and API access, VPC connections for data source access, VPC endpoints for AWS data services, and outbound access to required external domains.

Prerequisites

Before configuring private connectivity for Quick, make sure the following are in place:

  • An active AWS account with an Amazon Quick Enterprise subscription (VPC connections require Enterprise edition).
  • An existing VPC in the AWS Region where Quick is deployed.
  • A supported AWS Region. Quick website VPC endpoints are not available in the AWS China Regions or the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.
  • An AWS Direct Connect connection or Site-to-Site VPN established between your on-premises network and your VPC. This is the private path that carries traffic from your data center into AWS.
  • AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to create and manage VPC endpoints, security groups, and Quick administration. To create VPC connections, the administrator’s IAM identity also needs 
    quicksight:CreateVPCConnection
    , 
    quicksight:DescribeVPCConnection
    , 
    quicksight:ListVPCConnections
    , 
    quicksight:UpdateVPCConnection
    , 
    quicksight:DeleteVPCConnection
    , 
    ec2:DescribeSubnets
    , 
    ec2:DescribeVpcs
    , 
    ec2:DescribeSecurityGroups
    , 
    iam:ListRoles
    , and 
    iam:PassRole
    scoped to the VPC connection execution role.
  • Access to your organization’s DNS management (Route 53 private hosted zones or on-premises DNS forwarders), as private DNS resolution routes traffic through VPC endpoints rather than public addresses.

VPC endpoints for user and API access (AWS PrivateLink)

VPC endpoints powered by PrivateLink handle all user-facing traffic to Amazon Quick, including the website, API calls, and embedded content. They prevent users from needing to traverse the public internet to access the Amazon Quick console.

As shown in Figure 1: (1) a client on the corporate network sends a request to Quick; (2) the request travels over AWS Direct Connect, through the Direct Connect gateway, into your VPC; (3) the Quick VPC endpoint evaluates the endpoint policy and allows or denies the request; (4) allowed requests reach Amazon Quick over the AWS network.

Planning your VPC endpoint architecture

When planning your endpoint architecture, begin by identifying the AWS Region where your Quick account is deployed, as VPC endpoints must be in the same Region. Choose subnets across multiple Availability Zones for endpoint ENI placement, and make sure those subnets have routes to your on-premises network through Direct Connect or VPN.

Design security groups that restrict traffic on the endpoint ENIs to only required ports and source ranges. If you want all traffic routed privately (including the calls Amazon Quick makes to Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, and Amazon Athena), plan VPC endpoints for those services as well (see Configuring data source VPC endpoints).

Creating VPC endpoints for Quick

Quick requires two interface VPC endpoints for full private access:

  • Website access endpoint – Service name 
    com.amazonaws..quicksight-website
    . This handles the bulk of user traffic to the Quick console. Private DNS names for the Quick website differ from the public URL, so you must create an A record for 
    .quicksight.aws.amazon.com
    pointing to the VPC endpoint.
  • API access endpoint – Service name 
    com.amazonaws..quicksight
    . This handles programmatic API calls. When private DNS is enabled, existing API calls to 
    quicksight..amazonaws.com
    automatically route through the VPC endpoint with no additional DNS configuration. For FIPS compliance, use 
    com.amazonaws..quicksight-fips
    .

Note: Not every Quick API is available through the API VPC endpoint. The following 13 APIs are not supported: the action connector APIs (CreateActionConnector, DeleteActionConnector, DescribeActionConnector, DescribeActionConnectorPermissions, ListActionConnectors, SearchActionConnectors, UpdateActionConnector, UpdateActionConnectorPermissions) and the flow APIs (GetFlowMetadata, GetFlowPermissions, ListFlows, SearchFlows, UpdateFlowPermissions). Automation that manages action connectors or flows programmatically needs a path to the public API endpoint. See Quick and interface VPC endpoints.

If administrators sign in to Amazon Quick as IAM users through the VPC, also create the AWS Management Console endpoints:

  • com.amazonaws..console
    .
  • com.amazonaws..signin
    .

To create the website endpoint in the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) console:

  • Open the Amazon VPC console. In the navigation pane, under PrivateLink and Lattice, choose Endpoints, then choose Create endpoint.
  • Enter a Name tag (for example, my-quicksight-vpc-endpoint) and, for Type, choose AWS services.
  • Under Services, search for 
    com.amazonaws..quicksight
    and select 
    com.amazonaws..quicksight-website
    (Figure 2).
  • Under Network settings, select your VPC. Under Additional settings, keep Enable private DNS name selected.
  • Select subnets in at least two Availability Zones, then select the security group for the endpoint ENIs (Figure 3).
  • Choose a Policy (see the following Setting up VPC endpoint policies section), add tags, and choose Create endpoint (Figure 4).
  • Repeat these steps for the API endpoint, 
    com.amazonaws..quicksight
    .

Configuring DNS resolution

For the website endpoint, create an A record for 

.quicksight.aws.amazon.com
and point it to the VPC endpoint DNS name. This way, when users on your corporate network resolve the Quick URL, traffic routes through the private endpoint rather than the public internet. For the API endpoint, enabling private DNS on the VPC endpoint is sufficient, as API calls automatically resolve to the endpoint’s private IP addresses.

A Route 53 private hosted zone only answers queries from inside the VPCs associated with it. Because your users connect from the corporate network, configure your on-premises DNS servers to forward queries for 

.quicksight.aws.amazon.com
to a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC (or host an equivalent record in your on-premises DNS). Finally, validate DNS resolution from your corporate network to confirm that requests resolve to private IPs within your VPC rather than public addresses.

To create the record in Route 53:

  • In the Route 53 console, choose Hosted zones, then Create hosted zone.
  • For Domain name, enter 
    .quicksight.aws.amazon.com
    (for example, 
    us-east-1.quicksight.aws.amazon.com
    ). Scoping the zone to your Region avoids overriding other Quick host names. Choose Private hosted zone, associate your VPC, and choose Create hosted zone (Figure 5).
  • In the new hosted zone, choose Create record (Figure 6).
  • Leave Record name blank, choose record type A, turn on Alias, choose Alias to VPC endpoint, select your Region and the website endpoint’s DNS name, and choose Create records (Figure 7).

Setting up VPC endpoint policies

VPC endpoint policies restrict which accounts or organizations can use the endpoint. For Quick, policies can be scoped by AWS account ID or Organization ID. To change a policy, open the endpoint in the Amazon VPC console, choose the Policy tab, and choose Edit Policy (Figure 8).

Important limitation: For the Quick website endpoint, the 

Principal
, 
Action
, and 
Resource
fields must all be set to 
*
. Conditions might only be specified against the 
aws:PrincipalAccount
or 
aws:OrgId
attributes. More restrictive action-level policies are only supported on the API endpoint.

Website endpoint policy example:

API endpoint policy example (restricted to specific actions):

VPC connections for data source access

While VPC endpoints handle user-facing traffic, VPC connections handle the server-side path, meaning Amazon Quick reaches into your VPC to access databases, Amazon Redshift knowledge base sources, and internal APIs.

How VPC connections work

Amazon Quick Enterprise edition is fully integrated with Amazon VPC. When you create a VPC connection in Amazon Quick, you are adding elastic network interfaces (ENIs) into your VPC subnets. These ENIs allow Quick to exchange network traffic with resources within your VPC and, by extension, anything reachable from that VPC, including on-premises systems connected through Direct Connect or VPN.

All standard VPC security controls apply to this traffic. Route tables, network ACLs, subnets, and security groups govern traffic to and from Quick in the same way they govern traffic between any other instances in your VPC. This means you can connect to:

  • Private databases not exposed to the public internet.
  • On-premises data sources reachable through Direct Connect or VPN.
  • Internal APIs accessible by IP address within your network.

Create a dedicated security group (for example, 

QuickSight-VPC
) for the VPC connection ENIs. On each data source’s security group, allow inbound traffic on the database port from that security group ID.

Note for VPC connections created before April 27, 2023: The security group attached to the Quick network interface is not stateful. You must add an inbound rule that explicitly allows return traffic from your data source’s security group on all ports (0–65535), because return packets use randomly allocated destination ports. Connections created after that date use standard stateful behavior. See Security groups: inbound and outbound rules.

Creating the execution role

Amazon Quick doesn’t create the VPC connection execution role for you. Before you add the connection, create a dedicated IAM role (recommended), or update an existing role that already trusts Quick, such as 

aws-quicksight-service-role-v0
used in the screenshots in this post. The role needs:
  • A permissions policy that grants the Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) actions Quick uses to manage its ENIs (Figure 10).
  • A trust policy that allows 
    quicksight.amazonaws.com
    to assume the role. Only roles with this trust policy appear in the Execution role list in the Quick console.

Permissions policy:

Trust policy:

Configuring a VPC connection

To create a VPC connection in the Quick console:

  • Sign in to Amazon Quick as an administrator. Choose your profile icon in the upper-right, then choose Manage account (Figure 11). If you don’t see this option, you’re not a Quick administrator.
  • In the navigation pane, under Security, choose Manage VPC connections (Figure 12), then choose Add VPC connection.
  • Provide the following (Figure 13):
    • A descriptive VPC connection name.
    • The VPC ID of the target VPC. This can’t be changed later.
    • The Execution role you created in the previous step.
    • At least two subnets in different Availability Zones.
    • At least one security group ID.
    • (Optional) If your database host name must be resolved through private DNS, enter the IP addresses of your Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints under DNS resolver endpoints.
  • Choose ADD.

The connection status shows UNAVAILABLE until Quick finishes provisioning the ENIs, then changes to AVAILABLE. A status of PARTIALLY AVAILABLE means one of the ENIs is unavailable, but the connection can still be used.

Configuring data source VPC endpoints

VPC endpoints (PrivateLink, used here for AWS service APIs) and VPC connections (Quick ENIs placed in your VPC; see VPC connections for data source access) are different mechanisms. Quick accesses other AWS services (Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, Amazon Athena, AWS Secrets Manager) when retrieving data for dashboards and analytics. If you want all traffic to remain private, including the calls Amazon Quick makes to these AWS services, create interface or gateway VPC endpoints for each:

ServiceEndpoint typeService name
Amazon S3Gateway
com.amazonaws..s3
Amazon RedshiftInterface
com.amazonaws..redshift
Amazon Athena*Interface
com.amazonaws..athena
AWS Secrets ManagerInterface
com.amazonaws..secretsmanager
AWS GlueInterface
com.amazonaws..glue

* Athena isn’t supported as a VPC connection data source. The Athena endpoint keeps Athena API traffic on AWS PrivateLink only.

Create these endpoints in the same VPC where the Amazon Quick ENIs are placed. Make sure route tables and security groups allow traffic between the Amazon Quick subnets and the endpoint subnets.

Enabling access to required external domains

While data traffic between Quick and your on-premises sources stays on the private network, users’ browsers still need to reach a set of domains for sign-in, static assets, client-side metrics, and integrations. Even with VPC endpoints configured, domains without VPC endpoint support need outbound connectivity, typically through your corporate proxy or firewall. If your account uses IAM Identity Center, browser sign-in also requires the public AWS sign-in and IAM Identity Center endpoints (see Secure user access and identity federation).

Source: Domains accessed by Quick.

Configuration guidance:

  • For domains with VPC endpoint support (the Quick website and API, 
    signin.aws.amazon.com
    , and Amazon S3), create the corresponding VPC endpoints and DNS records.
  • For domains without VPC endpoint support, allow them through your corporate internet egress (outbound proxy or firewall). If user traffic egresses through your VPC, use a NAT gateway in a public subnet.
  • If your security posture requires URL-level filtering, use an outbound proxy or AWS Network Firewall domain filtering rules to allow only the domains listed earlier.
  • Test from a corporate workstation (or an instance in the same egress path): 
    nslookup
    and 
    curl
    against each domain confirm DNS resolution and routing.

Enforcing VPC endpoint restrictions

After your endpoints are configured and tested, you can enforce that all access to your Quick account must come through the VPC endpoint, blocking general internet access entirely. As a result, users can only reach Quick from your corporate network through the private path you’ve established.

Quick provides IP and VPC endpoint restriction controls that limit account access to a predefined list of IP ranges, VPC IDs, or VPC endpoint IDs. For example, you can create a rule that allows access only from the VPC endpoint used for Direct Connect, meaning anyone attempting to reach Quick from the public internet will be denied.

To configure through the Quick console (only administrators signed in with IAM credentials can access the restrictions page):

  • Choose your profile icon, then Manage account. Under Security, choose Manage IP/VPC restrictions.
  • In the Restriction field, enter the VPC endpoint ID (for example, 
    vpce-001122def
    ), enter a Description, and choose Add (Figure 14).
  • Choose Save changes to apply the rule.
  • Turn on Enforce restrictions.

Alternatively, configure through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI):

Note: 

UpdateIpRestriction
replaces the entire rule map. Retrieve your current rules with 
aws quicksight describe-ip-restriction
and include any existing rules in the update.

Key considerations:

  • IP and VPC endpoint rules apply to Quick web, embedded, and mobile access, meaning they don’t restrict access to the public API. To restrict API calls from specific sources, use IAM policies with 
    aws:SourceIp
    or 
    aws:SourceVpce
    conditions.
  • Make sure your own IP or VPC endpoint is included in the rules before enabling restrictions, otherwise you will lock yourself out.
  • Rules can take up to 10 minutes to take full effect.
  • You can combine IP rules and VPC endpoint rules, such that traffic is allowed if it satisfies either rule type. You can add up to 100 IP and VPC endpoint rules combined.
  • IP and VPC endpoint rules are enforced across all AWS Regions for your account, but you can only add or manage them from the AWS Region where your Quick account was created.
  • If you have publicly embedded dashboards, they will only be accessible through the VPC endpoint once restrictions are enabled.

After you enforce the restrictions, only traffic arriving through the specified VPC endpoint (or allowed IP ranges) can reach your Quick account. All other access is denied.

Secure user access and identity federation

Private network connectivity keeps traffic off the public internet, but it doesn’t answer the question of who can access what within Quick. This section covers how to integrate your corporate identity provider, control user provisioning, and enforce fine-grained access segmentation across Quick components.

Integrating with AWS IAM Identity Center

Important: For Quick accounts integrated with IAM Identity Center, browser-based authentication requires access to the public AWS sign-in and IAM Identity Center endpoints. VPC endpoints don’t provide this browser sign-in path. Public IP addresses aren’t required. Provide outbound connectivity through a NAT gateway or proxy. See Considerations for private access in the IAM Identity Center User Guide.

Amazon Quick uses AWS IAM Identity Center as the central point for workforce identity management. IAM Identity Center connects to your existing corporate identity provider (IdP) using SAML 2.0 for authentication and SCIM 2.0 for automatic user and group provisioning. This provides:

  • Automatic user provisioning and deprovisioning synced from your IdP.
  • Group membership synchronization – when a user is added to or removed from a group, that change propagates to Quick.
  • Single sign-on (SSO) using existing corporate credentials.
  • Temporary credentials through assumed IAM roles – no long-lived Quick-specific passwords.

For a step-by-step guide on setting up IAM Identity Center with your identity provider, see Getting started with IAM Identity Center.

Role-based access in Quick

Quick supports three base roles that determine what a user can do:

  • Admin – Full management access including data source configuration, VPC connections, security settings, user management, and SPICE capacity purchasing.
  • Author – Can create and publish dashboards, build agents, configure Spaces, manage data sources, create flows, and build apps.
  • Reader – Can view published dashboards, interact with agents, use Spaces they’ve been granted access to, and consume Quick Research reports.

These roles are mapped to IAM roles that federated users assume at sign-in. By managing role assignment in your IdP, you maintain a single source of truth for who has what level of access.

Additionally, Quick supports custom permissions profiles that can override default role permissions at the account, role, or user level. User-level permissions override role-level, which in turn override account-level. This gives administrators granular control beyond the three base roles.

User segmentation with Spaces

Quick Spaces provide an additional layer of access segmentation beyond roles. Each Space can be configured with specific user and group permissions, meaning:

  • A finance team Space containing sensitive revenue dashboards and financial knowledge bases is only accessible to the finance group.
  • A sales team Space with CRM-connected agents and pipeline dashboards is restricted to sales users.
  • Cross-functional Spaces can be shared across multiple groups with appropriate permissions.

Space-level access is controlled by the groups synced from your identity provider, so adding a new team member to the appropriate group automatically grants them access to the relevant Spaces.

Row-level security in Quick Sight

For dashboards backed by structured data, Quick Sight supports row-level security (RLS) that restricts which data rows each user or group can see. RLS is configured through dataset rules, which are a permissions dataset that maps users or groups to the field values they can access.

For example, a regional sales dashboard can be configured so that:

  • The EMEA sales group only sees rows where 
    region = 'EMEA'
    .
  • The NA sales group only sees rows where 
    region = 'NA'
    .
  • The VP of Sales sees all rows.

RLS rules are evaluated based on the user’s identity as determined by IAM Identity Center, meaning the same identity federation that controls sign-in also governs data-level access. This applies equally to traditional dashboard views and AI-powered natural language queries. The same security policies restrict what data the AI can reference when generating answers.

Column-level security

In addition to row-level restrictions, Quick Sight supports column-level security (CLS) to hide sensitive columns from specific users or groups. For example, a dataset containing employee information might restrict the salary and SSN columns to only the HR group, while other groups can still access non-sensitive columns in the same dataset.

How identity ties to private connectivity

The identity layer and network layer work together:

  • A user on the corporate network authenticates through your IdP → IAM Identity Center → Quick.
  • Their request reaches Quick through the VPC endpoint (the private network path; see VPC endpoints for user and API access).
  • Quick evaluates their identity to determine role, Space access, and RLS/CLS policies.
  • When Quick fetches data from an on-premises source, it uses the VPC connection (ENIs in your VPC; see VPC connections for data source access) to reach the database over Direct Connect.
  • The response is returned to the user through the same private path.

Apart from the sign-in and static-asset traffic described under Enabling access to required external domains, no traffic traverses the public internet, and at every point the user’s identity determines what they can see and do.

Validation and testing

Before enforcing restrictions in production, validate end-to-end connectivity for each access pattern:

Monitoring

For ongoing visibility, enable VPC Flow Logs on all endpoint and VPC connection ENIs to capture traffic metadata. Monitor CloudWatch metrics on VPC endpoints (

ActiveConnections
, 
BytesProcessed
, 
PacketsDropped
) and set alarms for connection failures or unexpected traffic sources. These logs also serve as the audit trail referenced in your compliance documentation.

Troubleshooting common issues

.quicksight.aws.amazon.com

For connections created before April 27, 2023, verify the inbound all-ports return-traffic rule. Check route tables for a path to the on-premises network.

Security best practices

Neither network isolation nor identity controls alone is sufficient. This architecture relies on both: network controls prevent unauthorized access paths, while identity controls prevent unauthorized data access within authorized sessions. The practices below maintain both layers.

  • Least-privilege endpoint policies: Restrict website endpoints by 
    aws:PrincipalAccount
    or 
    aws:OrgId
    . On API endpoints, scope policies to only the specific actions your automation requires rather than allowing all 
    quicksight:*
    actions.
  • Layered security groups: Apply security groups to both VPC endpoint ENIs (user traffic) and VPC connection ENIs (data traffic). On endpoint ENIs, restrict inbound HTTPS to your corporate CIDR ranges. On VPC connection ENIs, use a dedicated security group, restrict outbound to only the database ports and destinations Quick needs, and reference that security group in each data source’s inbound rules.
  • Enable VPC Flow Logs on all endpoint ENIs: These logs capture traffic metadata for security monitoring, anomaly detection, and compliance auditing. They also provide the audit trail that regulatory frameworks require for controlled network boundaries.
  • Audit endpoint policies regularly: Review endpoint policies quarterly. Use AWS Config rules to detect drift from your baseline configuration.
  • Separate VPC connections by sensitivity: If you have multiple data environments (dev, staging, production), create separate VPC connections with distinct security groups to prevent cross-environment access.
  • Monitor with CloudWatch: Set alarms on 
    PacketsDropped
    and 
    ActiveConnections
    metrics. Unusual patterns may indicate misconfiguration or attempted unauthorized access.

Example Requirements and AWS Configuration

The following examples show how the configuration in this post can address common security network requirements. Evaluate them against your own requirements with your security team.

RequirementAWS controls that can support your assessment
